observation.visible_scene: Nighttime waterfront: a dark sky above a still body of water that mirrors a distant lit shoreline, a slender central tower, and angled searchlight beams from the left. Multiple firework bursts occupy the upper-middle sky throughout the excerpt.
visible_changes: At the start (t=0–0.1s) three scattered dot-clusters (left pink/white, middle red, right blue-violet) are already spread out; over t=0.1–1.0s their points dim and thin, and individual sparks drift downward, so the clusters fade toward near-invisibility.

From about t=1.4s a new spherical-shell burst resolves in the center-left sky as an expanding ring of dots, followed by a second shell to its right; by t=2.0–2.5s these grow into well-defined radial spheres (a blue/violet shell left, a red/orange shell right, a smaller faint shell farther right).
These later shells expand radially and remain visible, slowly losing density, through the final frames (t=2.5–3.3s) rather than translating across the sky.

The water reflections track the sky: warm orange/white streaks dominate early, then violet-blue and red reflection patches appear and intensify as the spherical bursts bloom, with the reflected shapes wobbling and stretching due to surface ripples.

The shoreline, tower and searchlight beams keep fixed screen positions across all frames, indicating a static camera; apparent motion is from the fireworks and the water surface, not from camera movement.
outside_clip_unknowns: The launch/ignition of the initial dot-clusters occurred before t=0 (they are already mid-fade at the first frame).
The eventual dissipation of the spherical shells and any subsequent bursts lie beyond the last frame.
Whether the shells are fired from the unseen shoreline or from barges is not shown.
uncertain_details: Exact count and independence of overlapping shells is hard to separate where blue and red spheres touch.
Minor frame-to-frame shifts of the searchlight beams and reflections may be camera jitter or water motion; background landmarks appear stationary.
Some faint early dots in the top corners are too dim to confirm as fireworks versus stars or noise.
